fixes.why: The Leibniz test is a statement about the partial sums of a series, so it rests on the definition of series convergence; it was left with no needs at all.
The point asks the learner to see the Leibniz test as a special case of Dirichlet's test, so the Leibniz test must come first.
p65 in the nonnegative-terms piece is written explicitly as the idea behind the ratio test, deferring the full statement to this point; the cross-piece link was missing.
p65 is written explicitly as the idea behind the root test (a_n^(1/n) <= r eventually), deferring the full statement to this point; the cross-piece link was missing.

The positive and negative parts are a_n^+ = (|a_n| + a_n)/2 and a_n^- = (|a_n| - a_n)/2, and the proof that both converge exactly when the series converges absolutely uses the linearity of convergent series.
The Riemann rearrangement argument depends on the terms tending to zero, which makes the overshoot past the target shrink to zero; that comes from the term test.
Choosing a comparison series names logarithmic benchmarks among the options, and those are taught in p62.
Choosing a comparison series names geometric benchmarks among the options, and comparison with a geometric series is taught in p65.

Choosing a test for a general series builds on choosing a benchmark and a comparison method for nonnegative series (used on |a_n| when testing absolute convergence); without this link the two 'choosing' points sit in different pieces with no connection.

fixes.name: Logarithmic benchmark series
fixes.what: The learner can use the Cauchy condensation test to show that the sum of 1/(n log n) diverges (condensation turns it into a multiple of the harmonic series) and that the sum of 1/(n (log n)^p) converges exactly when p > 1 (condensation turns it into a p-series), and can repeat the step for series such as 1/(n log n log log n). From this ever slower chain of divergent series they see why no single benchmark list settles every series, which hints at the fact that there is no slowest divergent series.
fixes.why: The original said condensation is used twice for these series, but one application already turns them into the harmonic series and p-series; twice is needed only for log log terms. It also claimed these examples show there is no slowest divergent series, which they only suggest and do not prove.

fixes.name: Every number in [0,1] has a decimal expansion
fixes.what: The learner can prove that each x in [0,1) equals the sum of d_k/10^k by choosing digits greedily, d_k = floor(10^k x) - 10 floor(10^(k-1) x), and showing the k-th partial sum lies in (x - 10^(-k), x]. They handle x = 1 separately as 0.999... They know the expansion is unique except for numbers of the form m/10^k (with 0 < m/10^k <= 1), which have exactly two expansions, one ending in 0s and one ending in 9s.
fixes.why: The greedy floor recipe breaks at x = 1, where it would give a first digit of 10, so that case needs separate handling. The digit formula was also ambiguous ('10 times the previous one' reads as the previous digit), and the uniqueness statement did not say which numbers have two expansions.

verdict: The part is sound and covers its scope well. The test theorems are stated correctly, and the pieces link up properly now that the internal needs point to the right places, the missing cross-piece links are added (geometric comparison before the ratio and root tests, the benchmark-choosing point before the general test-choosing point) and two inaccurate point descriptions are corrected. The remaining open needs (sequence limits, limit laws, the monotone convergence theorem, Cauchy sequences, limsup and liminf, growth rates, logarithm properties, the triangle inequality, bijections and the Archimedean property) belong to the Sequences, Real numbers and Foundations parts and are left for the reviewer above.
